Incorporating SLOOS, the FOMC’s December 2022 statement reads even more restrictive than the baseline. While the statement already signaled a 50 bp hike, “ongoing increases,” and continued balance sheet runoff, SLOOS shows the transmission biting across credit channels:
- Broad-based tightening in bank lending standards for C&I and CRE, including construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, and multifamily; foreign banks also tightened C&I.
- Weaker loan demand from large, middle-market, and small firms, and softer demand in credit cards and auto; overall consumer loan demand mixed (some unchanged), but standards tightened for consumer and credit cards.
- Mortgage credit tighter across categories (including subprime and various jumbo/non-QM segments), though HELOC demand was stronger.
- Banks cited the economic outlook as a key reason for tightening, reported greater recession likelihood, and skewed approvals toward stronger borrowers (less likely to approve lower FICO, more likely for higher FICO).

Net: SLOOS corroborates and deepens the restrictive tone—credit supply tighter, demand softer, and recession risk elevated—amplifying the hawkish, credibility-focused stance of the FOMC. Minor offsets (unchanged auto standards, stronger HELOC demand) temper but do not change the overall restrictive reading.
